unit.title: JavaScript: first lines
unit.description: What JavaScript does, printing with console.log, text in quotes, numbers, comments

cards.definition: Prints a value in the browser console (F12), so you can see what your code is doing.
cards.example: console.log("Hello") shows Hello in the console.

cards.definition: A piece of text in JavaScript, written between quotes: "Hello" or 'Hello'.
cards.example: "42" between quotes is text, not a number.

cards.definition: A numeric value written without quotes, whole or decimal, that you can calculate with: 42, 3.5.
Text after // (one line) or between /* and */ that the computer ignores; it explains the code to humans.
cards.example: // Total with tax, written above a line, says what it computes.

cards.definition: One instruction for the computer, usually one line, often closed by a semicolon.
Capital and small letters are different in JavaScript: console and Console are two different names.

exercises.prompt: What is JavaScript used for in a web page?
choices: Making the page react: clicks, forms, changes
Choosing the colors and the layout
Writing the headings and the paragraphs
Hosting the website on the internet
exercises.explain: HTML is the content, CSS is the look, JavaScript is the behavior: it reacts to the user and changes the page.
whyWrong: Colors and layout are the job of CSS.
Headings and paragraphs are the job of HTML.
Hosting is done by a server, not by a language in the page.

exercises.prompt: What does this line show in the console?
exercises.explain: console.log() prints what is inside the parentheses. The quotes tell JavaScript that it is text.
whyWrong: The quotes only mark where the text starts and ends; they are not printed.
console.log is the command, not what it prints.
This line is valid: it prints the text.

exercises.explain: Numbers are written without quotes. 2 + 3 is computed first, then 5 is printed.
whyWrong: Without quotes, JavaScript computes the expression.
2 and 3 are numbers, so + adds them.
console.log prints the value without quotes.

exercises.explain: Between quotes it is a string: JavaScript prints it exactly as written, without calculating.
whyWrong: The quotes make it text: nothing is computed.
Nothing is added: it is one single piece of text.
It prints the text written between the quotes.

exercises.prompt: "42" (with quotes) and 42 (without quotes) are the same kind of value in JavaScript.
exercises.explain: "42" is a string (text) and 42 is a number. Only the number can be used in calculations.

exercises.prompt: What happens with the first line?
exercises.explain: // starts a comment: JavaScript ignores the rest of the line. Comments explain the code to humans.
whyWrong: Only the second line prints something.
A comment is valid code: it is simply skipped.
Comments never change how the code runs.

exercises.prompt: This code stops with an error. Which line is wrong?
exercises.explain: JavaScript is case sensitive: Console with a capital C does not exist. It must be console.log.

exercises.prompt: Build a line that prints the text Welcome in the console.
exercises.explain: console.log("Welcome"); the text goes between quotes, inside the parentheses.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is a string (a piece of text)?
exercises.explain: Text must be written between quotes: "blue" or 'blue'. Without quotes, JavaScript reads a name or a number.
whyWrong: Without quotes, blue is read as a name, not as text.
42 is a number.
3.5 is a number with a decimal point.

exercises.prompt: How many lines appear in the console?
exercises.explain: Each console.log prints one line, from top to bottom. The line that starts with // is a comment and never runs.
whyWrong: The third line starts with //: it is a comment and never runs.
Both lines without // run, one after the other.
The first two lines are normal instructions, so they run.
